1:
Who Arad was is unsettled, and Gill lays out the options, that the word names a place rather than a man, that Jerome knew the town as an Amorite city still shown near Hebron, and that Jarchi and the Targum of Jonathan take the attackers for Amalekites. Calvin argues that reading down at length, since the Amalekites had already failed once and were unlikely to try again with their own territory untouched, and since it would be absurd to call men descended from Esau Canaanites. His own answer is the Amorites, who were reckoned among the Canaanites by descent and whose borders reached to Mount Hor and Kadesh-barnea. Wesley reaches the same result more briefly, that the man is the Canaanite king of Arad and is called a Canaanite in the general sense, while Ellicott would render the whole verse afresh and leaves the date of the attack open.

The way of the spies divides them further. Clarke calls the obvious reading impossible and cites Kennicott, since Israel had already marched beyond Ezion-Gaber and were turning round Edom to the south-east, so that the word must be a place-name. Ellicott inclines the same way, allowing that Atharim may be a form of the word for those who searched the land but thinking it more probably a place occurring nowhere else. Wesley keeps the sense of spies but changes whose, taking them for scouts Israel sent to observe their own line of march, and Calvin agrees that men were sent ahead through unknown country as custom required, which is how Arad learnt that his territory was to be invaded.

Henry reads the attack as a miscalculation, that Arad thought it policy to keep the war at a distance and so meddled to his own hurt, since a people who might have been the last of the Canaanites destroyed became the first. Calvin sees providence in the smallness of the assault, that God accustomed Israel to conquest by degrees, since a combined attack by all these nations would have overwhelmed an unwarlike people at once. He and Wesley agree on why the first encounter went badly, that men who could not withstand a single people had to learn they were nothing without help from above. Both Henry and Calvin dwell on the vow that followed, Henry making it the pattern for asking mercy, that we should bind ourselves to honour God with the very thing we are seeking, and Calvin defending its apparent cruelty on the ground that it rested on a destruction God had already decreed, so that it was founded on his word, which is the first rule of vowing rightly.

Whether the vow was performed at once is the last question. Keil and Delitzsch think Israel could rest content with the defeat and defer the rest, since Moses never meant to force an entry into Canaan from the south across those mountains. Clarke goes further and suspects the verse was added after Joshua's day, since Arad appears among the cities Joshua destroyed long afterwards, though he allows that translating the verb as devoted to destruction would remove the difficulty without any such addition. Ellicott makes the same distinction and notes that the name Hormah is used by anticipation earlier in the book and was probably given afresh later, while Henry takes the name for a standing memorial, and hears it echoed in the Armageddon of the Revelation.
4:
Henry has no patience with the complaint, since men just victorious and with bread to spare still said there was no bread, and asks what will please those whom manna will not please. Clarke catches the tone of the word, calling it excessive scorn, this innutritive, cheat-stomach stuff, while Ellicott turns it on the reader, that the spiritual food given to Christ's Church is reckoned as cheap. Calvin works at the same word and thinks it means not light so much as vile, and observes that this rebellion had no new cause, where earlier ones at least had hunger or thirst behind them. Gill and Wesley press the phrase that they spake against God, taking it with the apostle for a speaking against Christ their conductor, while Keil and Delitzsch look at the ground under their feet, a plain of loose sand and drifted stone that would furnish almost nothing but the manna they were despising.

On the serpents the sources reach for natural history. Gill cites Aelian and Diodorus for scarlet serpents a span long whose bite was incurable, and Ellicott reports the rival explanations of the name, the red on their heads, the blaze of sun on their scales, or the burning of the bite. Clarke argues for the prester or dipsas against Bochart's water-snake, since that wilderness had neither rivers nor marshes, and quotes Lucan at length on the deaths of Aulus and Nasidius. Calvin thinks the creatures were made for the occasion rather than let loose, while Henry notes the justice of a thirst no water could quench given to those who complained for want of water.

Calvin makes the strangeness of the cure its whole point, since removing the serpents would have looked accidental and a plausible medicine would have obscured the grace. It is the peculiar virtue of faith, he says, that we should willingly be fools in order to be wise only from the mouth of God. Henry says the same of the refusal to grant what they asked, that God gives relief in the best way though not in our way, and Keil and Delitzsch add that the healing turned on the sufferer's faith in the promise. Gill supplies the practical detail, that Moses could have had his brass from Punon, the next station, which Jerome knew as a village where convicts worked the mines.

Wesley states the correspondence plainly, that the thing had the outward shape but not the inward poison, the pole answering to the cross and the looking to believing. Henry runs the parallel furthest, through the disease, the remedy and the application, ending on the promise that whoever looked from the outmost part of the camp with a weak and weeping eye was healed. Clarke will not have it, saying flatly that the brazen serpent was no type of Christ and that a serpent is the most exceptionable figure that could be chosen, though he grants five parallels from our Lord's own words. He and Ellicott both quote the Book of Wisdom, that the man who turned toward it was saved not by the thing he saw but by the Saviour of all.

Calvin dissents on a second point, that the lifting up is poorly explained as foreshadowing the crucifixion and belongs rather to the preaching of the gospel. His reason is the word itself, which means a standard or a mast, and Moses was told to set the thing on high to be seen from every side, answering Isaiah's promise of an ensign to the nations. Henry reaches the same word and makes it Christ lifted up on the cross and in the preaching alike, without choosing between them. Calvin and Ellicott close on the sequel, that a people so inclined to superstition ended by worshipping the thing, which Hezekiah ground to powder.
10:
Henry reads the list of stages as a quickening, a people near the promised rest setting forward, and wishes we would gain ground in the latter end of our own journey as they did. He notes how carefully they left Moab alone as the posterity of righteous Lot, camping on the side of Arnon the Amorites held, a scruple Jephthah pleaded on their behalf long after. Wesley uses the same fact to reconcile two commands that look contrary, since the land beyond Arnon had been Moab's but was now Sihon's, so taking it broke no promise to Lot's children. Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke fill in the ground, the Arnon running to the Dead Sea through a ravine walled by cliffs and choked with fallen stone, while Ellicott observes that the Hebrew does not say which bank they camped on.

The book of the wars of the Lord has attracted more conjecture than evidence. Gill reports Aben Ezra's view that it reached back to the battle of the kings in Abraham's day, and Wesley argues that quoting such a book prejudices nothing, since Moses might cite it as Paul cites heathen poets and Luke grants that many wrote histories never received as canonical. Clarke prefers Lightfoot's simpler guess, a book of remembrances Moses wrote for Joshua's instruction, possibly the book of Jasher. Keil and Delitzsch dismiss two modern accounts, an Amorite book of the conflicts of Baal and a work from Jehoshaphat's reign, and take it for odes from Moses' own time.

The words that follow Clarke calls impenetrably obscure, since scarcely two versions agree and our own translators pushed the hard words into the margin untranslated. He reports Calmet's conjecture, adopted by Houbigant, that copyists' slips turned Zared into Vaheb, which would yield an itinerary instead of a riddle. His own preference is to take the clause for a proverb of distance like from Dan even unto Beersheba. Calvin rejects the search for a book altogether, holding the phrase means only that the place would be celebrated whenever the wars of Jehovah were recounted, and reads Vaheb as a verb rather than a town, so that God fought as gloriously at Arnon as he began at the Red Sea.

At Beer the supply came differently, and Keil and Delitzsch mark it, that here God commanded wells to be dug rather than striking water from a rock. Henry makes much of the silence before it, that their bottles were spent and yet they did not murmur, so God gave before they asked, and that in this world we pitch in Oboth where comforts lie in scanty vessels while heaven is the well itself. Calvin doubts this is the old rock, since Paul says the Rock followed them, by which he understands not that it was torn from its roots but that God drew the water on after them. Henry and Calvin draw the same lesson from the digging, that God promised the water but they had to open the ground for it, the excellency of the power being still his.

Clarke will not accept the picture of princes digging a well with walking-sticks, and re-translates the song so that they searched it out and the nobles digged it upon their own borders. Ellicott keeps the staff but makes it the ruler's sceptre, and reports that the Targums read the next verses not as marches but as the travels of the well itself, which descended with Israel into the valleys and rose to the heights. Gill adopts that reading too, noting the places named are absent from the list of encampments and so were passed through rather than pitched in. Wesley and Henry close on the figure, that as the serpent lifted up stood for Christ, so this well stands for the Spirit poured out.
21:
Keil and Delitzsch set the embassy beside the earlier one to Edom and mark the difference in what followed, since God had forbidden war on the kinsmen of Israel but commanded it against the Amorites, whose iniquity was ripe. They add that the offer of peace was still made in earnest, so that the decision of Sihon's fate was left in his own hand, and Wesley agrees that Israel meant what they said and would have kept to the high road. Henry finds the answer worse than Edom's, since the Edomites had only refused passage and stood on their defence, where Sihon marched out beyond his own borders unprovoked and so ran himself upon his ruin. He and Gill both trace that folly past Sihon's politics to the hardening of his spirit, Henry adding that the enemies of the church are often infatuated in the very counsels they think most wisely taken.

Henry alone works out the question of title, and does it twice over. Against the Amorites he allows that their aggression alone might not have entitled Israel to the country, and rests the claim instead on the grant God made to Abraham, to be executed when the iniquity of the Amorites should be full, the same ground Jephthah pleaded long afterwards. Against the Moabites, who had held the land before, he supplies what he calls a replication for posterity, that the Amorites had taken it from Moab some time before and Israel therefore took it from Amorite and not from Moabite hands. From this he draws two reflections, on the uncertainty of possessions which change owners so often and make themselves wings, and on a providence that had lodged the country with the Amorites beforehand, who little thought they held it only as trustees until Israel came of age.

Where the conquest stopped is explained by three of the sources in the same direction. Ellicott takes the note about the strength of the Ammonite border as a reason why the Amorite advance was arrested, not why Israel spared Ammon, since Israel had been forbidden to meddle with them at all. Wesley reads it the same way and adds that Sihon could not push his conquests eastward as he had pushed them against Moab, whether the obstacle was the river or the fortresses on the frontier. Keil and Delitzsch fix the limits geographically instead, from the Arnon to the upper Jabbok, the stream still called the blue.

What Israel then did with the country divides on a single word. Ellicott argues that dwelt should be rendered sojourned or abode, of a temporary encampment, since the permanent settlement east of Jordan came only after the death of Moses. Calvin reaches the same conclusion from the other end, that God had not yet declared them masters of this side of the river and that they would have overpassed their bounds had he not added it to their inheritance. He explains the destruction of the cities as deliberate policy rather than cruelty of their own, since a people already inclined to be slothful had to be denied a comfortable resting-place, so that the very desolation might urge them on to where God was calling them.
26:
Gill and Wesley give the plain reason for the note about Heshbon, that Israel took the country from Amorite and not from Moabite hands and so held it justly. Calvin makes far more of it, arguing that Moses inserted this piece of history into the record deliberately, because three hundred years later the Ammonites would use the old ownership as a pretext for war, and Jephthah would answer them out of exactly this passage. He then raises a question the others do not, why it was the king of Ammon rather than of Moab who pressed that claim, since the song itself shows the land was taken from Moab. His answer is that men bent on plunder find any trivial pretext sufficient and will often glory in other men's rights, passing over in silence what the lapse of ages has buried.

Who the makers of proverbs were interests three of the sources. Gill takes them for the historians of the Amorites, poets who put the wars into verse as Homer did the wars of Troy, and wrapped their matter in short enigmatic sayings so that it might be the better remembered, while Jarchi names Balaam and Beor. Clarke derives the word from a root meaning to rule, since a weighty saying was received as an axiom for the government of life, and ranges these men alongside the poets of Greece and Rome, the shaara of the Arabs, the bards of the Druids and the Sennachies of the Celts. Wesley is less interested in who composed it than in why it is quoted, as proof that the land was Sihon's and as evidence of God spoiling the spoilers.

Clarke divides the ode into three parts, an ironic celebration of Sihon's insults over the beaten Moabites, a lament over Moab with a sarcasm against a god who abandoned his worshippers, and finally Israel's own revenge, and prints the whole in hemistichs from Kennicott. Keil and Delitzsch count three strophes likewise, and identify Chemosh as the chief god of Moab and Ammon, which Jerome took for another name of Baal Peor and probably a sun-god worshipped as king and god of war. Wesley breaks with both, holding that the Amorite song ends before the woe upon Moab and that what follows is Israel's own comment upon it, scoffing at the impotence not of the Moabites only but of their god. Calvin reads the opening summons as men calling each other to Sihon's standard, takes the command to build as a promise to enlarge and enrich a city not yet fallen, and suggests that the lords of the high places may be the idols themselves, since the conquerors were elated enough to despise the gods of the vanquished along with the men.

On the fire that went out of Heshbon the sources agree it means the war itself, Gill citing the Jerusalem Targum for a people mighty and burning like fire, and Wesley observing that a city which had been the country's refuge became its plague. Calvin takes the word rendered light or lamp in the last strophe more widely still, for the whole substance of a prosperous state, so that the boast is that their glory and their wealth alike were annihilated. Wesley closes the ode on the Amorites with the shortest verdict in the chapter, that the triumphing of the wicked is short. Gill ends where the narrative does, calling the settlement the beginning of the conquest and an earnest of the inheritance, though Ellicott would still render the verb sojourned rather than dwelt.
32:
Gill and Wesley agree on Jaazer, that it was another town the Amorites had taken from Moab and now lost in their turn, Gill adding from Jerome that it lay fifteen miles from Heshbon and returned to Moabite hands long afterwards. Keil and Delitzsch note that the narrative never says from what point Israel set out against Bashan, and are content to leave it so, since the detail was of no importance to the writer's purpose. Wesley offers a guess about the two kings, that Sihon and Og may have led two colonies out of Canaan which drove out the earlier inhabitants of that country. He and Calvin both dwell on the land itself, famous for its pastures and its cattle and its oaks, and Calvin remarks how great a favour it was to gain so wide and fertile a territory in what amounted to a moment.

Gill explains the encouragement given before the battle by Og's gigantic stature and the numbers he brought, which might well have frightened Moses and the people. Calvin argues the opposite way round, that although Israel had the larger force the king would not have marched out unless he thought himself equal to resistance, so that God's grace shone the more conspicuously in the result. Keil and Delitzsch treat the promise as the counterpart of the one given about Sihon, and note that the ban was executed on both kings alike, so that no remnant was left. Gill and Calvin both close the account on the scale of the conquest, sixty cities walled and barred besides the open towns, which fell to the half tribe of Manasseh.

Calvin alone asks why so much of it was then destroyed, and answers that a fertile country with convenient houses would have tempted a people to settle short of the rest God had promised them. Men who had once been ready to turn back to Egypt, he says, would have taken possession of such a land eagerly and reposed in it as in a delightful nest, so the desolation was what compelled them to move on. He observes that the land was in the end granted to Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh, but on the condition that they leave their herds behind and go with their brethren until the Canaanites were destroyed. He also notices that the command is addressed to Moses alone though meant for all, since a man already energetic needed less spurring than the rest.

Clarke closes the chapter with a long appendix from Kennicott, who calls several of its verses as now translated remarkably unintelligible. Two of the difficulties Kennicott removes from the Greek, which makes the way of the spies a proper name and the vow a devoting to destruction at some future time, so that the march need not be read as a vast and unnecessary detour. A third he removes by denying that Mattanah, Nahaliel and Bamoth are stations at all here, since the verbs of journeying and pitching are absent and the words follow lines of verse, so that they mean the gift, the torrents of God and the high places, a traveller's shout of joy at finding water in plenty near the end of the road. He places Suph not at the Red Sea but near the meeting of Arnon and Jordan, reading the line as saying that the God who brought Israel through the sea of Suph had now brought them to Suph again, and Clarke adds Lightfoot's curiosity that Psalm 136 rehearses God's mercy twenty-six times, the number of the generations from Adam to Moses and of the letters of the divine name.
